UBASE: An AI Search Engine for Trillion-Scale Vector Data Management at ByteDance

Yao Tian†, Yuncheng Lu†, Liyao Xiong, Yuming Xu, Hao Zhang*, Weichen Zhao Xi Zhao, Bo Kuang, Dongyu Wang, Jiehui Li, Yakun Li*, Lei Zhang ByteDance
Abstract.

Since 2016, UBASE has been the foundation of ByteDance’s search infrastructure, scaling to more than 7,000 clusters and 300 PB of indexed data. Driven by the demands of AI workloads, UBASE has evolved from a text search engine into a unified AI search system supporting vector retrieval, lexical matching, and predicate filtering. Its largest deployment indexes nearly one trillion high-dimensional vectors. This scale exposes two central bottlenecks in AI-era retrieval: memory-intensive graph-index construction under sustained ingestion, and the prohibitive cost of keeping vector indexes entirely in memory.

UBASE addresses these bottlenecks with two techniques. First, it introduces a quantization-aware vector kernel based on SymRaBitQ, a new symmetric quantization scheme with tight theoretical guarantees that allows index construction to run directly in the quantized space accurately and efficiently without retaining a copy of full-precision vectors. Second, it provides a hybrid storage engine that supports memory-resident, hybrid, and SSD-resident deployments, with fine-grained record-level caching to trade memory for latency under operational control. On large-scale benchmarks, UBASE improves throughput by up to 3×3\times, reduces indexing memory by 80%80\%, and lowers operating cost by 86%86\% compared with prior systems, while supporting trillion-vector scale, write-heavy or latency-sensitive workloads in production.

22footnotetext: Equal contribution: {yao.tian, luyuncheng}@bytedance.com.11footnotetext: Corresponding authors: {zhanghao.ai, liyakun.hit}@bytedance.com.

1. Introduction

UBASE11 1 UBASE originated from an early OpenSearch branch; we thank the community for its foundational contributions. has served since 2016 as ByteDance’s core search infrastructure. Today, UBASE manages more than 7,000 clusters and over 300 PB of storage. AI applications, such as retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis et al., 2020), recommendation (Li et al., 2018; Peng et al., 2024), semantic analytics (Patel et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024), and conversational assistants (GitHub, Inc., 2023; Cursor, 2024), have driven UBASE to evolve from text-based search engine to AI search engine, where vectors are first-class indexed data and queries combine vector similarity with lexical matching, structured predicates, and reranking.

Vector data growth is multiplicative rather than incremental. As shown in Fig. 4, UBASE is storing vectors at an exponential rate, while Fig. 4 shows two production workloads each ingesting several billion new vectors per day. Our largest clusters are already nearing trillion-vector scale with PB-scale storage footprints. The demand is rising along three coupled axes: granularity, dimensionality, and retention. Retrieval units are becoming finer-grained, e.g., video search moving from scene-level to frame-level embeddings; newer encoders are increasing embedding dimensionality from 128 to 2048; and vectors are being stored for longer periods, e.g., AI-memory workloads extending retention from 45 to 365 days. These trends compound: each application may generate more vectors per user, store wider vectors, and retain them for longer. Consequently, vector data management has shifted from a component-level optimization to a PB-scale system-level optimization.

Vector data is resource-intensive and challenging to manage. Unlike scalar fields, each vector is a dense object that is expensive to store, index, and query. A 2048-dimensional FP32 vector occupies 8 KB, so 100 million vectors require 800 GB of raw storage before indexing. Vectors are usually partitioned into random segments during ingestion22 2 Production vector engines such as OpenSearch/ElasticSearch (OpenSearch Project, 2024; Elastic NV, 2024) and Milvus (Wang et al., 2021) commonly adopt segment-based index management, which supports high-throughput vector ingestion while simplifying incremental addition and deletion in deployed systems., and indexes are built over them. Index construction for these vectors is memory- and compute-intensive. For example, building a graph-based vector index (vs. HNSW - Exploring ANN algorithms Part 1, 2022; Jayaram Subramanya et al., 2019), typically the fastest option for vector search, for a 1-million-vector segment requires at least 8 GB of memory and takes over one hour. Querying, in other words, finding the approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) vectors to a query vector, is similarly expensive: graph-based methods employ a greedy traversal to progressively move toward vertices closer to the query. Each hop takes at least 1 random I/O, and there could be 100+ hops to reach 95% recall in a single segment, and it must search all segments.

At trillion-vector scale, with ingestion and serving running concurrently, memory becomes the central constraint: every byte spent on index construction is a byte unavailable for serving. Our production workloads in §2 expose two bottlenecks. First, ingestion amplifies memory usage: index builders must retain full-precision vectors until segment finalization, so at 10+ billion vectors ingested per day and peaks above 700K vectors/s, naive construction can consume tens of terabytes and exhaust cluster memory. Second, serving becomes I/O-bound because memory-only serving is economically infeasible, making SSD-backed serving necessary at a trillion-vector scale33 3 VM memory costs roughly 61×\times more per byte than SSD storage. A typical VM instance with 8 GB memory is priced at ≈\approx 6.7$/GiB-month, versus an SSD-backed block device is priced at 0.10$/GiB-month.. Cache efficiency is therefore critical: misses on graph neighbors or vectors trigger SSD reads, increasing tail latency and reducing throughput.

These problems cannot be avoided by moving vector search into an isolated service. Customers require OpenSearch compatibility to preserve existing APIs, dashboards, access control, ranking pipelines, and operational playbooks,44 4 Many customers are migrating from OpenSearch-based lexical search to hybrid search that combines vector, lexical, and structured retrieval; preserving OpenSearch compatibility is therefore essential. while also demanding hybrid queries that combine vector similarity, lexical matching, structured predicates, and reranking. Existing systems miss one side of this requirement. Faiss (Faiss, 2025) provides efficient ANN kernels but lacks distributed ingestion, durability, and operational control. Milvus (Wang et al., 2021) provides an integrated vector service but does not match OpenSearch’s mature lexical and ranking ecosystem. OpenSearch and Elasticsearch (OpenSearch Project, 2024; Elastic NV, 2024) provide the right ecosystem, but their vector paths hit memory and I/O bottlenecks at trillion-vector scale. This leaves a practical gap: production hybrid search needs OpenSearch compatibility and extreme-scale vector performance in the same system.

We present UBASE, a production-grade search engine for AI workloads built inside the OpenSearch/Elasticsearch ecosystem. Rather than proposing a standalone vector service, UBASE replaces the quantization, storage, and query-execution paths that become bottlenecks at extreme scale, enhances hybrid search ability, enables unified storage between memory-only, hybrid, and disk-only deployed mode, while preserving existing APIs, DSLs, dashboards, and operational playbooks. Its design follows from a deployment constraint: at trillion-vector scale, the hard problem is not only low-latency ANN search, but sustaining ingestion, index, storage, and hybrid query execution within an operational search platform.

UBASE addresses these challenges through two design choices. First, compression is integrated into the indexing path. Full-precision vectors otherwise dominate memory consumption during index construction, so UBASE introduces SymRaBitQ (§4), a symmetric quantization scheme with solid theoretical guarantees. Its unbiased, error-bounded distance estimator operates directly on quantized codes, eliminating full-precision vector copies and substantially reducing indexing cost. Second, storage placement is adaptive and optimized for cache efficiency. Production clusters span memory-rich, memory-constrained, and SSD-heavy deployments, and their cost–latency trade-offs change with workload. UBASE supports memory-resident, hybrid memory-disk, and SSD-resident execution within the same system, using fine-grained record-level caching and asynchronous graph traversal optimized for SSD I/O patterns (§5). Both design choices are integrated into an OpenSearch-compatible architecture that preserves support for rich predicates, ranking functions, and hybrid retrieval workloads (§6). Together, these choices make UBASE a drop-in evolution of existing search infrastructure rather than a parallel vector stack, closing the gap between ecosystem maturity and trillion-scale AI retrieval without requiring migration or abandoning operational tooling. On large-scale benchmarks, UBASE delivers up to 3×3\times higher throughput, 80%80\% lower indexing memory, and 86%86\% lower operating cost compared to state-of-the-art systems while preserving recall and latency. In production, UBASE supports both PB-scale write-heavy clusters and latency-sensitive online serving clusters within the same operational ecosystem.

In summary, this paper makes the following contributions:

  • •

    We distill the production insights from ByteDance’s AI search platform–7 000+ clusters, 300+ PB storage, trillion-scale vectors–identifying memory-efficient graph construction during ingestion and vector storage during serving as the two dominant physical bottlenecks at extreme scale.

  • •

    We introduce SymRaBitQ, a quantization scheme with strong theoretical accuracy guarantees, and a quantization-aware vector kernel that enables search, graph construction, and segment merge entirely in the quantized space.

  • •

    We design an adaptive storage engine supporting memory-resident, hybrid, and SSD-resident vector indexes with fine-grained cache management for efficiently utilizing cache in trillion-scale vector workloads, and a hybrid query engine that integrates vector, lexical, predicate, and reranking operators within a single distributed query plan.

  • •

    We evaluate UBASE on public benchmarks and production deployments up to 838 B vectors and 3 PB of storage, achieving up to 80%80\% lower graph-build peak memory, 60%60\% faster build time, and 7.3×7.3\times lower storage cost while preserving recall and latency.

2. Production Workload & Challenges

2.1. Production Workloads

Table 1 summarizes representative UBASE workloads across 7000+ clusters/services with over 300 PB storage. Customers first adopted UBASE as an OpenSearch-compatible platform, then incrementally enabled vector search over existing queries and workflows. Consequently, UBASE cannot expose vector search as a standalone ANN service: it must preserve query semantics, shard/segment management, filtering, ranking, and hybrid retrieval across memory- and SSD-resident indices. Workloads expose overlapping features:

  • •

    Hybrid queries. Customers A–F combine vector similarity with lexical, scalar, and domain-specific predicates, then apply ranking and LLM-based recall. Their cost is therefore dominated not by ANN traversal alone, but by materialization, filtering, merging, and downstream reranking. These workloads require end-to-end hybrid query optimization.

  • •

    Low-latency online serving. Memory-resident workloads, such as A, B, C, and F, target p99 latencies in the tens to hundreds of milliseconds for high-dimensional vector queries.

  • •

    PB-scale ingestion & serving. Disk-resident workloads, such as D and E, operate at PB scale, where the memory-only option is economically infeasible. Their query requirements are comparatively relaxed: both QPS and tail latency remain modest, as shown in Fig. 4 and Fig. 4. The primary challenge is sustaining ingestion and serving over massive datasets.

System requirements.   These workloads impose three requirements on UBASE.

  • •

    OpenSearch-native hybrid execution. UBASE must preserve the OpenSearch compatibility—including ingestion, segment merge, replication, recovery, monitoring, query DSL, filtering, ranking, and shard-level execution—while making vector search a first-class operator inside the same distributed query plan.

  • •

    Unified memory–SSD backend. UBASE must support memory-resident, SSD-resident, and mixed deployments with one architecture. As Table 1 shows, production deployments span 105–212 TiB memory-backed workloads and 2–3 PB SSD-backed workloads, so the system cannot rely on a DRAM-only ANN design or a separate disk-specialized serving path.

  • •

    Large-scale continuous ingestion and serving. UBASE must sustain hundreds of billions to trillions of vectors under continuous writes while serving queries in reasonable times. At this scale, ingestion-side index construction and serving-side cache management contend for the same memory, making ingestion and serving a coupled system problem rather than two independent pipelines.

2.2. Challenges

At the trillion-vector scale, DRAM is the shared bottleneck between ingestion and serving. In practice, naïve graph construction can transiently consume more memory than the final index itself. For Customer E, construction peaked at 27 TB against a 13.8 TB DRAM budget, making the system infeasible even before reserving memory for the serving-side caches needed to hide SSD latency. This exposes a fundamental trade-off: allocating DRAM for fast ingestion inflates peak memory, while leaving too little for caching slows query throughput. Two interdependent challenges emerge:

  • •

    Excessive peak memory during graph construction. Conventional builders retain full-precision vectors, candidate neighborhoods, pruning state, partial edges, and metadata until segments are finalized, inflating peak memory. The challenge is reducing this peak without fragmenting segments or degrading index quality, ensuring that SSD traversal remains efficient downstream.

  • •

    Ineffective DRAM use for SSD-resident graph search. Trillion-scale indices cannot fit in DRAM, so queries traverse SSD-resident graphs, vectors, and metadata. The challenge is that DRAM capacity alone does not determine performance: cached data only helps when it avoids SSD accesses on the query-critical path. Without traversal-aware cache allocation, scarce DRAM can be spent on bytes with low latency impact, while hot graph regions still trigger SSD reads.

Limitations of existing systems.   Disk-based ANN in OpenSearch and Elasticsearch (OpenSearch Project, 2024; Elastic NV, 2024) reduces serving-time DRAM with better binary quantization (BBQ) (Trent, 2025), but leaves the ingestion–serving memory conflict unresolved. On the ingestion side, BBQ is asymmetric: its compressed representation is used for search, but graph construction still materializes full-precision vectors and construction metadata, directly competing with serving caches for DRAM. On the serving side, generic mmap/page caches operate at page granularity and cannot prioritize ANN records on query-critical traversal paths. UBASE addresses this shared bottleneck by quantized construction (§4), and a fine-grained DRAM–SSD cache (§5), reducing ingestion peak memory and converting the freed DRAM into higher serving-cache efficiency, while preserving full opensearch compatibility and support rich predicates, filtering, and ranking options (§6).

3. System Overview

Fig. 5 shows the UBASE architecture. Externally, it preserves full OpenSearch compatibility: clients, REST APIs, SDKs, ingestion pipelines, dashboards, and index lifecycle tools work unchanged. This lets existing deployments adopt UBASE without rewriting workflows.

Internally, UBASE treats vectors as first-class citizens. Instead of treating vectors as add-ons, it co-designs vector representation, storage layout, and hybrid query execution to boost search efficiency while keeping OpenSearch’s robustness for non-vector workloads.

The engine redesign targets three core components for production-scale vectors:

  • •

    Quantization-aware vector kernel (§4): SymRaBitQ enables distance estimation, index construction, and segment merge without repeated full-precision materialization.

  • •

    Adaptive storage engine (§5): controls segment lifecycle, memory/SSD placement, caching, and async I/O, addressing the large memory-to-SSD cost gap in production.

  • •

    Hybrid query engine (§6): unifies vector similarity, lexical relevance, structured predicates, score fusion, and reranking within an OpenSearch-compatible distributed plan.

Ingestion & Query Workflow.   UBASE separates write freshness from serving efficiency. Newly refreshed data first becomes searchable as lightweight fresh segments, while background merge bounds query fanout and progressively upgrades segments from raw vectors, to IVF indexes, to graph indexes. For graph-indexed segments, UBASE builds and merges directly in the SymRaBitQ quantized space, avoiding repeated full-precision vector materialization. The segment abstraction also decouples indexing from placement: the same index can serve from DRAM, hybrid memory–SSD, or SSD-resident storage without reindexing. Appendix A details the ingestion path.

On the read path, UBASE preserves native DSL semantics but executes hybrid retrieval as one distributed plan. BM25, vector search, predicates, range filters, score fusion, and reranking are optimized together rather than stitched across separate services. The query engine is placement-oblivious: DRAM segments use in-memory traversal, while SSD-resident graph records use a record-level buffer pool and asynchronous traversal to overlap I/O with distance computation. Appendix B details the serving paths, and Appendix C shows a representative native DSL query.

4. Quantization-Aware Vector Kernel

Existing SOTA quantization schemes, such as RabitQ/BBQ (Gao and Long, 2024; Trent, 2025), are asymmetric: they quantize data vectors but evaluate them against full-precision query vectors. Thus, they do not directly support quantized-domain data-to-data distance evaluation, which UBASE needs during index construction. Falling back to full precision would require an extra uncompressed data copy, which amplifies memory usage. UBASE therefore introduces SymRaBitQ, a symmetric scheme that unifies data-to-query and data-to-data evaluation in the same quantized-space primitive.

4.1. SymRaBitQ Quantization

SymRaBitQ is the distance primitive used by the UBASE vector kernel. It keeps the high-accuracy RaBitQ/ExtRaBitQ code construction (reviewed in Appendix D.1) and changes the estimator so that both operands may be represented by compact codes. Throughout this section, raw vectors are denoted by 𝒙r,𝒒r∈ℝD\bm{x}_{r},\bm{q}_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}. When a vector is encoded relative to a centroid 𝒄\bm{c}, e.g., in IVF or partitioned graph indexes, UBASE uses normalized residuals

(1) 𝒐:=𝒙r−𝒄‖𝒙r−𝒄‖,𝒒:=𝒒r−𝒄‖𝒒r−𝒄‖.\small\bm{o}:=\frac{\bm{x}_{r}-\bm{c}}{\|\bm{x}_{r}-\bm{c}\|},\hskip 18.49988pt\bm{q}:=\frac{\bm{q}_{r}-\bm{c}}{\|\bm{q}_{r}-\bm{c}\|}.

We write 𝒐¯\bar{\bm{o}} and 𝒒¯\bar{\bm{q}} for their quantized representations, and store for every encoded data vector the residual norm ρ𝒐=‖𝒙r−𝒄‖\rho_{\bm{o}}=\|\bm{x}_{r}-\bm{c}\| and the self-correlation γ𝒐=⟨𝒐¯,𝒐⟩\gamma_{\bm{o}}=\langle\bar{\bm{o}},\bm{o}\rangle. Algorithm 1 summarizes the encoding path used for both data and query residuals. The variable 𝒙\bm{x} is instantiated as 𝒐\bm{o} for stored vectors and 𝒒\bm{q} for queries.

Symmetric estimator.   Given two encoded residual unit vectors, SymRaBitQ estimates their inner product as

(2) ⟨𝒐,𝒒⟩^=⟨𝒐¯,𝒒¯⟩⟨𝒐¯,𝒐⟩​⟨𝒒¯,𝒒⟩.\small\widehat{\langle\bm{o},\bm{q}\rangle}\;=\;\frac{\langle\bar{\bm{o}},\bar{\bm{q}}\rangle}{\langle\bar{\bm{o}},\bm{o}\rangle\,\langle\bar{\bm{q}},\bm{q}\rangle}.

For data-to-data comparisons, both denominator terms are precomputed; for query-to-data comparisons, only ⟨𝒒¯,𝒒⟩\langle\bar{\bm{q}},\bm{q}\rangle is computed online once. The corresponding squared L2L_{2} distance used by the graph and IVF kernels is

(3) SymDistB⁡(𝒐¯,𝒒¯,𝒄)=ρ𝒐2+ρ𝒒2−2​ρ𝒐​ρ𝒒⋅⟨𝒐,𝒒⟩^,\small\operatorname{SymDist}_{B}(\bar{\bm{o}},\bar{\bm{q}};\bm{c})=\rho_{\bm{o}}^{2}+\rho_{\bm{q}}^{2}-2\rho_{\bm{o}}\rho_{\bm{q}}\cdot\widehat{\langle\bm{o},\bm{q}\rangle},

where BB denotes the bit width of the code. Inner-product search is handled by the same estimator after applying the standard residual reconstruction terms.

Code-only computation.   The numerator ⟨𝒐¯,𝒒¯⟩\langle\bar{\bm{o}},\bar{\bm{q}}\rangle in Eq. (2) is computed directly from the integer codes, not by materializing rotated floating-point vectors. For B=1B=1, the computation reduces to sign agreement and can be evaluated with bit operations and popcount. For the B=5B=5 construction code used in UBASE, it becomes a compact integer-code dot product; the graph and IVF kernels below call Eq. (3) directly rather than a generic full-precision distance.

Accuracy guarantee.   SymRaBitQ preserves the accuracy properties needed by an ANN kernel: the estimator is unbiased and has an O⁡(1/D)O(1/\sqrt{D}) error bound with high probability.

Theorem 1 (SymRaBitQ Estimator).

For normalized residual vectors 𝐨\bm{o} and 𝐪\bm{q},

Proof Sketch.

We decompose the estimation error into two residual terms and bound each using high-dimensional concentration arguments. Unbiasedness is established using the near-orthogonality of random transformations and the expected sign agreement between quantized vectors. Full proofs are provided in Appendix E and Appendix F. ∎

Remark 1.

Compared with RaBitQ, SymRaBitQ appears to introduce only a modest mathematical modification. However, this change has important system implications. RaBitQ accelerates query-time estimation, whereas graph construction and segment merging require a large number of distance computations over stored vectors. By moving both operands into the quantized space, SymRaBitQ eliminates raw-vector accesses for these data-to-data computations, extending the benefits of quantization from the query path to the entire index construction and maintenance lifecycle. Appendix D.1 provides additional background on RaBitQ.

4.2. Graph-based Kernel

Large merged segments in UBASE use a DiskANN/Vamana-style graph because the construction cost is amortized across many future queries (§2); the graph background and full pseudocode are given in Appendix D.2. Our contribution is not a new graph topology. The graph kernel keeps DiskANN’s candidate discovery, robust pruning, and backward-edge repair, but changes the representation and every distance oracle used by these steps.

Quantization-aware Construction.   Before graph construction starts, each assigned vector is encoded as a SymRaBitQ record z𝒐=(𝒐¯,𝒐¯0,γ𝒐,ρ𝒐)z_{\bm{o}}=(\bar{\bm{o}},\bar{\bm{o}}_{0},\gamma_{\bm{o}},\rho_{\bm{o}}), where γ𝒐=⟨𝒐¯,𝒐⟩\gamma_{\bm{o}}=\langle\bar{\bm{o}},\bm{o}\rangle and ρ𝒐=‖𝒙r−𝒄‖\rho_{\bm{o}}=\|\bm{x}_{r}-\bm{c}\| are precomputed. After this point, the graph builder no longer calls a full-precision distance function. In FindCandidates (Algorithm 3), the greedy frontier is ranked by SymDistB\operatorname{SymDist}_{B} between encoded records. In RobustPrune (Algorithm 4), both target-to-candidate distances and candidate-to-candidate diversity checks also use SymDistB\operatorname{SymDist}_{B}. Backward-edge repair uses the same pruning routine when a neighbor exceeds the degree bound. Algorithm 2 shows the complete construction flow. This change is precisely where SymRaBitQ differs from a query-only quantizer. Standard RaBitQ can score a quantized data vector against a raw query, but robust pruning needs distances among stored vectors, such as d⁡(𝒐,𝒗)d(\bm{o},\bm{v}) and d⁡(𝒑,𝒗)d(\bm{p},\bm{v}). Without a symmetric estimator, these comparisons would fetch raw candidate vectors from disk or keep them in memory. With SymRaBitQ, all such comparisons read only BB-bit codes and per-vector scalars, so graph construction operates in the quantized space.

Quantization-aware Search.   The query path uses the same record format. A query is encoded once for the searched partition, producing z𝒒=(𝒒¯,𝒒¯0,γ𝒒,ρ𝒒)z_{\bm{q}}=(\bar{\bm{q}},\bar{\bm{q}}_{0},\gamma_{\bm{q}},\rho_{\bm{q}}). During greedy traversal (Algorithm 5), UBASE uses SymDist1\operatorname{SymDist}_{1} on the first-bit projections 𝒐¯0\bar{\bm{o}}_{0} and 𝒒¯0\bar{\bm{q}}_{0} to expand the graph with a bit operation plus SIMD popcount (vpopcntq). Only the small promising set retained by traversal is rescored with SymDistB\operatorname{SymDist}_{B} using the full code. Thus construction uses the higher-precision BB-bit estimator to preserve graph quality, while search uses a coarse-to-fine version of the same estimator to reduce memory bandwidth and CPU work.

Impact.   The immediate effect is that raw vectors are removed from candidate search, pruning, backward-edge repair, and most graph-search distance computations. The memory footprint of construction becomes proportional to compact codes plus graph metadata rather than high-dimensional floating-point vectors; random I/O to raw vectors is eliminated from the recurring merge path. In our implementation, B=5B=5 preserves more than 98% distance-estimation accuracy and causes less than 0.01 recall loss under the same search parameters. On GIST-1M (Table 2 in §7), SymRaBitQ reduces peak build memory by 80% and total build time by 60%, demonstrating the significant benefits of quantization for index construction.

4.3. IVF-based Kernel

For medium-size segments (§2), UBASE builds an IVF index because it is cheap to construct and the segment may still participate in later merges. IVF background is given in Appendix D.3; the key point in the vector kernel is that IVF list construction and list scanning also use SymRaBitQ as the distance primitive.

Index primitives.   UBASE first quantizes all vectors with SymRaBitQ using the segment centroid. The entire kk-means clustering procedure then operates in the quantized space via SymDistB\operatorname{SymDist}_{B}. The quantized codes (𝒐¯,𝒐¯0,γ𝒐,ρ𝒐)(\bar{\bm{o}},\bar{\bm{o}}_{0},\gamma_{\bm{o}},\rho_{\bm{o}}) are stored in their assigned inverted lists, while full-precision vectors remain on disk and are no longer needed for list construction or later segment merge. This keeps medium-segment indexing lightweight while preserving the same compressed representation used by graph segments.

Search primitives.   At query time, UBASE encodes the query with SymRaBitQ and probes the closest n𝑝𝑟𝑜𝑏𝑒n_{\mathit{probe}} centroids in the IVF index. For each probed centroid, we evaluate SymDist1\operatorname{SymDist}_{1} on 1-bit codes to obtain coarse distances using vpopcntq. Candidates whose lower bounds are already worse than the current kk-th result are discarded without touching the remaining bits. The survivors are refined with SymDistB\operatorname{SymDist}_{B} using FastScan-style lookup tables (André et al., 2015; André et al., 2017; André et al., 2021), and the top-kk heap is updated. In this path, SymRaBitQ improves both bandwidth and CPU efficiency: most list entries are judged by compact 1-bit codes, and only promising entries pay for the full BB-bit estimate.

5. Vector Storage Engine

UBASE’s storage engine manages the lifecycle of vector segments beneath the OpenSearch-compatible interface. At a high level, it makes newly written segments searchable at refresh time, bounds query fanout through background merges, upgrades per-segment indexes from scan to IVF and then to graph-based search, and places each segment on memory-only, hybrid memory–disk, or disk-resident serving paths. We inherit OpenSearch’s data layout; the ingestion path is described in Appendix A.

The rest of this section focuses on the optimizing of serving disk-resident segments inspired by (Zhao et al., 2026). Sec. 5.1 introduce fine-grained cache mechanism that largely reduces disk I/Os. Sec. 5.2 describes the asynchronous execution model that reduces tail latency by overlapping graph traversal with SSD reads.

5.1. Fine-Grained Record Cache

Given the cache-efficiency problem, UBASE must spend limited DRAM on data that actually advances graph traversal. Traditional page-granular caching is too coarse for graph search: it can spend DRAM on incidental bytes that do not advance traversal. UBASE therefore employs fine-grained, record-level caching. Each record stores the compact vector payload for distance estimation and a bounded neighbor list for traversal. As shown in Fig. 6, a dense record-mapping array indexed by vertex ID gives O⁡(1)O(1) access to each record through pointer-swizzling-style logical pointers (Leis, 2024). Each entry of the record-mapping array is a 64-bit logical pointer consisting of a residency bit, a 2-bit state field, and a 61-bit offset. An MSB of 0 indicates that the record is on disk and the offset is the disk-page offset; an MSB of 1 indicates that the record is cached in memory and the offset is the slot offset in the slotted buffer region. The state field records transient cache states, which UBASE uses to coordinate record loading, prefetching, and eviction under concurrent queries. To manage these operations, UBASE uses a lightweight lock-free protocol. On a miss, the requester locks the disk-resident mapping entry, obtains a free slot or runs clock-style eviction, issues a non-blocking SSD read, copies the fetched record into the slot, and publishes the memory-slot offset as an occupied resident record. Concurrent demand loads or prefetches that observe the disk entry in the locked state wait for the same load to complete rather than issuing duplicate reads. During eviction, the clock hand first demotes occupied resident entries to marked; a later access promotes the marked entry back to occupied, while an unaccessed marked entry can be locked, its slot reclaimed and returned to the free list, and its mapping entry restored to the disk location.

5.2. Asynchronous ANN Execution

Fine-grained caching improves DRAM utilization, but cache misses can still occur during graph traversal. UBASE treats those misses as scheduling points inside the SSD-resident vector operator. Each ANN search runs as a coroutine that carries its candidate frontier, visited vertices, and current top-kk results. The traversal is cache-aware at the candidate-beam level: it expands resident candidates first when they are available, while issuing asynchronous reads or prefetches for promising on-disk candidates. If no ready candidate can make progress, the coroutine yields after submitting the required SSD read. The worker then advances another ready ANN coroutine and resumes the suspended search when the read completes. This design complements the record cache: the cache reduces avoidable SSD traffic, while coroutine scheduling overlaps the remaining SSD latency with useful vector-search computation.

6. Hybrid Query Engine

Production workloads (§2) are rarely plain top-kk ANN retrieval: they often combine vector similarity with lexical matching, structured predicates, ranking, reranking, and threshold-based retrieval. To support diverse workloads efficiently, UBASE integrates vector search into an OpenSearch-compatible distributed query engine. The coordinator parses the DSL, routes the request to shards, and composes vector operators with the rest of the search pipeline. We refer the reader to Appendix. B and Appendix C for query path details and example DSL that enables hybrid query. For the rest of this section, we focus on three concrete techniques that enhance three kinds of specific hybrid queries.

Vector + Full-text Search.   Production workloads often benefit from combining lexical matching, which excels at exact term retrieval, e.g., searching logs by error codes, with vector search that captures semantic relationships beyond literal expressions.UBASE provides flexible hybrid retrieval within a unified query framework, where query terms are processed through Lucene’s inverted index with BM25 scoring and query embeddings are evaluated by the vector search engine. Users can choose from multiple score normalization strategies, including min-max, L2, z-score, and reciprocal rank fusion (RRF), as well as several score fusion methods, such as weighted arithmetic mean, geometric mean, and harmonic mean. These configurable options allow fine-grained control over the balance between lexical and semantic signals, enabling retrieval behavior to be tailored to different applications and relevance objectives.

Radial Search.   Radial search is useful when applications specify similarity or distance constraints rather than a fixed top-kk. Recommendation workloads, e.g., Customer C, often require retrieving results within a relevance threshold (e.g., max_distance or min_score) while excluding near-duplicates via an exclusion threshold (e.g., min_distance or max_score). To efficiently support these query patterns, UBASE designs a threshold-guided neighborhood expansion strategy on graph-based indexes. The search starts from an entry point obtained via a top-1 ANN lookup and expands neighbors in a breadth-first manner, interleaving threshold evaluation with traversal. Nodes satisfying the bound are emitted and recursively explored, while others are pruned early. The search terminates when the frontier is exhausted or when a system-defined exploration limit is reached, ensuring bounded work while preserving recall within the specified range.

Filtered Vector Search.   Production workloads often include structured predicates such as tenants, categories, tags, timestamp ranges, and access-control policies. UBASE supports three filtering modes: pre-filtering, post-filtering, and in-filtering. Pre-filtering applies predicates before vector search and is effective for highly selective conditions, while post-filtering evaluates predicates after ANN retrieval and is suitable for low-selectivity predicates. When neither strategy is effective, UBASE enables an in-filter execution mode. The predicate is first materialized as a bitmap over valid vector IDs, and ANN search retrieves a small set of high-similarity seeds. The vector operator then expands from these seeds while checking the bitmap on the fly, admitting only qualifying candidates. Expansion continues until sufficient valid results are collected.

7. Experiment

We evaluate UBASE using public benchmarks and production-derived workloads on a controlled testbed. Production deployment results are presented in Sec. 2. Specifically, our evaluation answers six production-facing questions:

  • Q1:

    Can quantization-aware vector kernel in UBASE reduce recurring indexing cost, improve the QPS–recall frontier, and lower tail latency? (§7.2)

  • Q2:

    Can a unified engine efficiently support filtered, hybrid, and radial retrieval? (§7.3)

  • Q3:

    Does UBASE improve the operating-cost envelope? (§7.4)

  • Q4:

    Can the storage runtime mask SSD stalls under constrained memory and smoothly transition between disk-resident and memory-resident serving? (§7.5)

  • Q5:

    Does UBASE scale with data size and cluster size? (§7.6)

  • Q6:

    Can UBASE sustain stable read–write performance during prolonged streaming ingestion? (§7.7)

7.1. Experiment Setup

Datasets.   We use one production-derived dataset and six public datasets. The production-derived dataset is a 100M-vector sample from Customer D, the 327B-vector deployment described in Sec. 2. Together with Wiki (1M, 768D, cosine) (Dataset, 2023), GIST (1M, 960D, L2) (Dataset, 2010), and Cohere (113M, 1024D, L2) (Dataset, 2024), these datasets are used to evaluate throughput, latency, recall, and index construction cost. For end-to-end hybrid retrieval quality, we use NFCorpus, FIQA, and Quora from a popular benchmark BEIR (Thakur et al., 2021; Kamalloo et al., 2024).

Competitors.   We compare our system with three well-known specialized and generalized vector databases: Elasticsearch 8.1855 5 https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch, Milvus 2.566 6 https://github.com/milvus-io/milvus, and PostgreSQL 1777 7 http://www.postgresql.org/ with the VectorChord 1.0 extension88 8 https://github.com/tensorchord/VectorChord/. Elasticsearch is a distributed search and analytics engine that has recently incorporated vector search via an HNSW-based index with BBQ (Trent, 2025). Milvus is a widely used specialized vector database, providing high-performance ANN search with multiple indexing algorithms (e.g., IVF, HNSW, SQ). PostgreSQL with VectorChord represents the trend of integrating vector search into relational databases, enabling ANN search within SQL-based hybrid workloads.

Environment and Configurations.   Our controlled benchmarks run on machines equipped with Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8457C CPUs. UBASE is deployed as an OpenSearch-compatible cluster with three data nodes and two coordinator nodes. For smaller-scale datasets (Wiki and GIST), each data node uses 8 CPU cores, 64 GB of memory, and 1 TB of network-attached storage, and each coordinator node uses 8 CPU cores and 16 GB of memory. For large-scale datasets (Cohere and In-house), each data node uses 24 CPU cores, 192 GB of memory, and 2 TB of network-attached storage, and each coordinator node uses 16 CPU cores and 32 GB of memory. Storage is connected via 10 Gigabit Ethernet. Baseline systems are provisioned under comparable resource budgets and tuned according to their recommended practices. Unless otherwise stated, all results use the default per-system resource and index settings reported in Appendix G.

Evaluation Metrics.   We report Queries Per Second (QPS) latency, and Recall@kk for query performance, and normalized discounted cumulative gain (NDCG) for end-to-end ranking quality. Recall is defined as

(8) R​e​c​a​l​l​@​k=|R∩R∗|k,\small\vskip-4.62497ptRecall@k=\frac{|R\cap R^{*}|}{k},

where RR denotes the returned top-kk results and R∗R^{*} denotes the exact top-kk results for a query. NDCG is defined as

(9) 𝑁𝐷𝐶𝐺​@​k=𝐷𝐶𝐺​@​k𝐼𝐷𝐶𝐺​@​k,𝐷𝐶𝐺​@​k=rel1+∑i=2krelilog2⁡(i),\small\mathit{NDCG@k}=\frac{\mathit{DCG@k}}{\mathit{IDCG@k}},\hskip 9.24994pt\mathit{DCG@k}=\mathrm{rel}_{1}+\sum_{i=2}^{k}\frac{\mathrm{rel}_{i}}{\log_{2}(i)},

where reli\mathrm{rel}_{i} denotes the relevance score of the result at rank ii, and 𝐼𝐷𝐶𝐺​@​k\mathit{IDCG@k} is the maximum possible D​C​G​@​kDCG@k under an ideal ranking. We measure indexing performance by construction time, peak memory consumption, and index size. We also report query cost per million queries and estimated in-house storage cost for cost-effectiveness.

7.2. Indexing & Vector Search Performance

This subsection evaluates whether UBASE reduces index-construction cost and improves high-recall serving efficiency.

Indexing.   We evaluate the recurring cost of index construction along three dimensions: build time, peak memory, and final index footprint. Table 2 isolates the effect of SymRaBitQ on the construction path by comparing UBASE’s quantization-aware construction with DiskANN and HNSW, the graph-construction backends used by systems such as Milvus and OpenSearch/Elasticsearch. DiskANN builds the graph over full-precision vectors, whereas UBASE constructs the graph directly in the quantized space. On GIST 1M, SymRaBitQ reduces build time from 587 s to 237 s (60%60\%). Of the 237 s, 43 s is spent on quantization and the remaining 194 s on graph construction in the quantized space. Peak memory is simultaneously reduced from 3.75 GB to 0.75 GB (80%80\%). The same effect holds at production scale: on Cohere 100M, build time drops from 23,826 s to 12,496 s (48%48\%), while peak memory drops from 453 GB to 90 GB (80%80\%). These results show that SymRaBitQ is not merely a query-time compression technique; it moves quantization into the recurring build and merge path, cutting the memory spikes that contend with online serving during continuous ingestion.

The effect is not limited to graph construction. SymRabitQ also reduces the cost of IVF indexing. On GIST 1M, conventional IVF requires 176 s and 3.7 GB peak memory, while SymRaBitQ-enhanced IVF reduces build time to 129 s (27%) and peak memory to 1.9 GB (49%). Since IVF shows similar behavior, we omit further IVF results and focus subsequent experiments on graph indexing, which dominates both indexing complexity and serving performance in UBASE.

Fig. 7 further shows that UBASE achieves the smallest end-to-end index footprint across datasets. The reason is architectural: because UBASE constructs a high-quality graph directly over high-precision quantized vectors, full-precision vectors are no longer needed in the hot serving path and are kept only in remote storage for durability and offline maintenance. On Wiki, UBASE’s index is 1,182 MB, only 29%29\% of PostgreSQL and 42%42\% of Milvus, the most space-efficient baseline. The trend persists on the 100M-scale datasets, where retaining full-precision or weakly compressed vectors directly increases serving footprint and storage cost.

Vector Search.   We next evaluate whether UBASE improves the throughput–recall and tail-latency–recall frontiers. Since recall above 90%90\% is a common target in our production workloads, we focus on this high-recall regime and compare against Elasticsearch, Milvus, and PostgreSQL/VectorChord.

Fig. 9 shows that UBASE moves the QPS–recall frontier rather than improving only one operating point. On the in-house 100M dataset, UBASE reaches 21,445 QPS at around 90%90\% recall@10, which is 9.5×\times higher than Milvus, 5.5×\times higher than PostgreSQL, and 2.3×\times higher than Elasticsearch. As recall increases, the baselines degrade rapidly around 92%92\% recall, while UBASE still sustains over 10K QPS. On Cohere, UBASE reaches 23,013 QPS at around 92%92\% recall@10, outperforming Milvus by 11.7×\times, Elasticsearch by 5.4×\times, and PostgreSQL by 3.5×\times.

On smaller datasets such as GIST 1M and Wiki 1M, the gap narrows because most systems can keep a larger fraction of the working set in memory and avoid frequent disk I/O. Nevertheless, UBASE remains on the best QPS–recall frontier. On GIST, it is up to 5×\times faster than PostgreSQL and more than 2×\times faster than the second-best Milvus configuration. On Wiki, it reaches nearly 25K QPS at 87%87\% recall and still sustains around 15K QPS at 97%97\% recall. Although the second-best baseline changes across datasets, UBASE consistently provides the best frontier.

The improvement comes from three design choices. First, UBASE uses a vector-native execution path integrated into the OpenSearch query pipeline, avoiding redundant data movement and cross-engine coordination. Second, UBASE adopt a quantization aware vector kernel, where distance computation is performed in the quantized space using fast scan operations such as vpopcnt, reducing per-query computation cost. Third, the quantization scheme preserves distance fidelity well enough to sustain high recall under aggressive pruning and high-QPS settings. Fig. 9 shows the corresponding concurrent p99 latency results: at comparable recall, UBASE also maintains lower tail latency than the baselines. Together, the throughput and latency results show that UBASE improves the high-recall serving frontier on both axes. Additional average, p95, and serial-latency results are reported in Appendix I.

7.3. Complex Query Performance

This subsection evaluates whether UBASE can efficiently support diverse retrieval workloads. We focus on three representative query patterns: filtered search (vector + attribute filters), hybrid search (vector + lexical matching), and radial search (similarity-threshold retrieval).

Filtered Search.   Fig. 10 reports QPS at approximately 96% recall@10 as predicate selectivity varies from 10% to 99%. We make four observations. First, UBASE consistently achieves the highest throughput across the entire selectivity spectrum. Second, all systems experience throughput degradation relative to pure vector search. Although scalar filtering itself is inexpensive, its overhead becomes significant when vector search latency is already only a few milliseconds. Third, throughput decreases as predicates become more selective. With fewer candidates satisfying the predicate, ANN search must explore a larger portion of the graph to collect enough valid results. Finally, at the extreme selectivity of 99%, UBASE exhibits a noticeable throughput advantage. This is because UBASE automatically switches to pre-filtering when the estimated candidate set falls below a configurable threshold (10,000 in this experiment). The middle and right panels provide a finer-grained comparison at 50% and 70% selectivity. Across all recall levels, UBASE consistently delivers higher throughput than competing systems, demonstrating the effectiveness of its adaptive filtering strategy.

Hybrid Search.   Table 3 evaluates end-to-end retrieval quality by comparing traditional lexical retrieval (BM25), dense vector retrieval, and three score-fusion strategies supported by UBASE’s query engine in Sec. 6. The results show that lexical and semantic signals are complementary: fusion consistently outperforms BM25 and dense retrieval alone. No single normalization strategy dominates across all datasets. Z-score fusion performs best on FIQA and Quora, improving NDCG@10 by 65.5% and 16.9%, respectively, while RRF performs best on NFCorpus with a 43.3% improvement.

Radial Search.   This experiment evaluates the radial search algorithm introduced in Sec. 6. As shown in Fig. 11, we vary the radius so that the search region contains approximately {10​k,20​k,50​k,100​k}\{10\text{k},20\text{k},50\text{k},100\text{k}\} vectors, and evaluate both the 100M in-house dataset and a random 1M subset. A naive implementation that emulates radial search with kNN at k∈{10​k,20​k,50​k,100​k}k\in\{10\text{k},20\text{k},50\text{k},100\text{k}\} does not finish within the one-minute timeout. In contrast, UBASE’s threshold-guided neighborhood expansion returns 10K results in 140 ms on both datasets. Even at 100K returned results, latency remains practical: 3.68s on the 100M dataset and 1.2s on the 1M subset. These results show that radial search can support large-range queries without reducing them to repeated large-kk ANN calls.

7.4. Operating Costs

Table 4 reports the monthly operating cost for serving the 100M 2048D dataset, using the deployment configuration in Appendix  H. We report cost per 1M vectors for keeping the dataset online and cost per 1K QPS for buying serving throughput. In the memory-only case, all systems use the same monthly budget of 27902790: Milvus, PG, and ES reach 2262, 3929, and 9342 QPS, respectively, while UBASE reaches 21445 QPS, improving over ES by 2.3×2.3\times and reducing serving cost to 130 per 1K QPS. In the disk-only case, UBASE targets minimum standing cost rather than peak throughput, reducing monthly cost to 382382 and cost per 1M vectors to 3.7, which is 7.5×7.5\times lower than the memory-only baselines, while still serving 63 QPS for low-duty-cycle or archival workloads. Overall, the experiment shows that UBASE is cost-saving in both end of operating modes: maximizes throughput under a fixed budget or minimizes the cost of keeping a large vector collection online.

7.5. Storage Runtime Analysis

This subsection evaluates UBASE’s storage runtime for SSD-resident vector search using controlled ablations. Experiments are conducted on a single 48C371GiB serving, fixing recall at 90%. We isolate the effects of record-level caching and asynchronous execution, and then vary the buffer-pool ratio to measure the smooth memory–throughput transition.

Record-Level Cache Effectiveness.   We first evaluate whether the record-level cache described in Sec. 5.1 reduces SSD traffic during graph traversal. Fig. 12 and Fig. 14 compare DiskANN with UBASE (-sync), which enables the 20%-size record cache. UBASE-sync consistently outperforms DiskANN as the thread count increases, indicating that record-level caching effectively eliminates a large fraction of random SSD accesses. Fig. 14 quantifies the resulting I/O savings. UBASE achieves a 97.7% cache hit rate on GIST. Although each query visits 105.99 graph records on average, only 51.90 SSD accesses per query are required (I/O misses + prefetches), compared to 80.9 for DiskANN. Similar benefits are observed on the in-house dataset, indicating that the effectiveness of record-level caching persists at larger scales.

Asynchronous Execution Effectiveness.   Fig. 12 evaluates the impact of asynchronous execution. UBASE-async issues graph-record fetches asynchronously and switches to other ready query coroutines while I/O is outstanding, whereas UBASE-sync uses the same cache mechanism but waits synchronously on cache misses. As the number of worker threads increases, UBASE-async scales substantially better than UBASE-sync. At 32 threads, it achieves roughly 15K QPS, about 1.8×\times higher than UBASE-sync and 2×\times higher than DiskANN. At the same time, UBASE-async maintains an average latency of approximately 1.7 ms, while UBASE-sync and DiskANN increase to about 3.5 ms and 4 ms, respectively. These results show that asynchronous execution complements the record cache by turning remaining graph-record I/O stalls into useful inter-query overlap.

Smooth Memory–Throughput Transition.   We further evaluate whether buffer-pool sizing provides a continuous performance knob across storage configurations. We vary the buffer-pool ratio from 0% to 100% on the in-house dataset, using a fixed thread count of 12. As shown in Fig. 14, increasing the buffer ratio from 0% to 10% improves throughput from 4,163 to 5,381 QPS (1.29×\times), showing that a small memory budget can already absorb many hot-record accesses in SSD-resident workloads. At a 10% buffer ratio, UBASE reaches roughly 70% of the peak throughput at 100% (7,701 QPS). Throughput then improves monotonically as the buffer ratio grows, giving operators a smooth path from capacity-oriented SSD-resident deployments toward memory-resident high-QPS deployments without changing the query interface or rebuilding the index.

7.6. Operational Scaling Behavior

This subsection evaluates whether UBASE provides predictable serving performance as data volume and cluster resources change.

Data-Scale Scalability.   We first examine how UBASE scales as the indexed data grows. We construct datasets by randomly sampling {1​M,10​M,20​M,…,100​M}\{1\text{M},10\text{M},20\text{M},\ldots,100\text{M}\} vectors from the in-house collection while keeping the serving configuration unchanged. For each data scale, index parameters are tuned to meet the same 90% recall target, and the corresponding QPS is measured. As shown in Fig. 16, QPS decreases gradually as the dataset grows, reflecting the increased cost of candidate selection and distance evaluation. Notably, the degradation remains smooth and approximately logarithmic: when the dataset size increases by two orders of magnitude, from 1M to 100M vectors, QPS decreases by only 9%, from 24,410 to 22,386. This behavior is consistent with the logarithmic scaling characteristics of graph-based similarity search and provides a predictable performance envelope as collections grow.

Node-Scale Elasticity.   Fig. 16 further evaluates whether UBASE can translate additional data nodes into higher serving throughput. We vary the number of data nodes from 1 to 10 on the in-house dataset and measure the QPS achieved at the same recall target. As shown in Fig. 16, UBASE achieves near-linear throughput growth as more data nodes are provisioned. This trend is expected given UBASE ’s OpenSearch-based architecture: queries are coordinated and executed in parallel across shards hosted on data nodes, and each additional data node contributes additional CPU, memory, and I/O bandwidth to process its share of shard-level ANN search. With balanced shard allocation and stable per-shard index structures, the workload is effectively partitioned and processed independently. As a result, cluster-level throughput scales approximately proportionally with the number of data nodes, until secondary bottlenecks (e.g., coordination overhead or network bandwidth) begin to dominate.

7.7. Streaming Micro-benchmark

We finally evaluate whether UBASE can sustain stable serving performance during continuous ingestion. We run a 30-hour micro-benchmark on Cohere: vectors are inserted from an empty index at a fixed rate of 1,000 vectors/s, while read queries are issued concurrently under fixed system configurations and index parameters. We continuously monitor query throughput, ingestion throughput, and P99 read/write latencies throughout the run. As shown in Fig. 18, UBASE sustains the configured ingestion rate throughout the run while keeping query QPS stable, showing that background indexing and segment maintenance do not noticeably disrupt foreground search. Fig. 18 reports the P99 read and write latencies over the same period. Both remain stable, indicating that continuous writes do not introduce frequent read-path latency spikes or write-side backpressure. We attribute this stability to UBASE’s fast indexing path and controlled merge process. By accelerating segment construction and merge, UBASE prevents many small streaming segments from accumulating, which would otherwise increase query fan-out and hurt read performance. Overall, these results show that UBASE provides predictable read–write performance under prolonged streaming workloads.

8. Lessons

We distill five lessons from building and operating UBASE.

Lesson 1: Innovate within compatibility boundary.   Compatibility shaped UBASE end-to-end, from API surface to index lifecycle, distributed execution. The lesson is to keep the boundary stable and innovate inside it: UBASE preserves OpenSearch-facing behavior while redesigning the vector kernel and storage underneath. A standalone vector service might be cleaner, but it would export operational complexity to every application team. Production teams already operate 7,000+ clusters with existing APIs, dashboards, alerts, access controls, and playbooks.

Lesson 2: Quantize the build path, not just the query path.   Many vector systems apply quantization at query time but still rely on full-precision vectors for index construction. In a system with sustained ingestion (Customers D, E), index construction is a recurring production path, and its memory footprint and construction time matters as much as the query-time memory usage and speed, as it will compete the memory and computation resource for serving. SymRaBitQ enables graph construction and merge entirely in the quantized space. In our experiments (Table 2), this reduced peak build memory by 80% and indexing time by 60% on GIST 1 M, with less than 0.01 recall loss under the same search parameters.

Lesson 3: Bridge the cost gap with I/O co-design, not just tiered storage.   The 60×\times memory-to-SSD price gap makes memory-only serving unsustainable for large corpora such as Customer D’s with near trillion-scale vectors. However, simply placing graph data on SSD hurts tail latency because graph traversal has sparse, pointer-chasing access patterns that break page-level caching. UBASE addresses this with record-level buffer pools and asynchronous graph traversal. In our cache-sensitivity experiment (Fig. 14), a 10% buffer ratio already achieves ∼\sim70% of peak memory-resident throughput, showing that a small, well-targeted cache can bridge most of the performance gap.

Lesson 4: Make storage placement a tunable segment property.   Production workloads evolve: what starts as a latency-sensitive service may need to shift toward cost-effective SSD-resident serving as retention or data granularity grows. UBASE avoids this becoming a migration event by making storage placement a per-segment property controlled by buffer pool sizing.

Lesson 5: Compose retrieval operators in one plan.   In production, it is common that vector similarity is composed with structured predicates, lexical matching, and reranking (Customers A-F). Executing these operators in one distributed plan avoids materializing large intermediate results and enables end-to-end scheduling that a multi-service pipeline cannot provide.

9. Related Work

We briefly review core methods and system designs for vector systems. For detailed surveys, we refer the reader to (Song et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2024).

Vector Search Algorithms.   Existing ANN methods can be broadly categorized into three groups: LSH-based methods (Gionis et al., 1999; Huang et al., 2015; Tian et al., 2022; Zheng et al., 2020), graph-based methods (Dong et al., 2011; Malkov and Yashunin, 2020; Fu et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2023a; Subramanya et al., 2019), and quantization-based methods (Jégou et al., 2011; Gao and Long, 2024). In modern vector databases, graph-based methods such as HNSW (Malkov and Yashunin, 2020) and DiskANN (Subramanya et al., 2019) are highly effective for ANN search. They build approximate proximity graphs that capture neighborhood relationships among data points, enabling accurate and efficient query processing. Nevertheless, their high construction cost and substantial random memory/disk accesses often motivate the use of quantization-based methods, such as PQ (Jégou et al., 2011) and RaBitQ (Gao and Long, 2024), to reduce computation and memory footprint.

Architectures for Vector Data Management.   Production-grade vector search is increasingly closer to a full data management system than to a standalone ANN operator (Faiss, 2025). Beyond similarity search, systems are expected to provide scalable storage and layout management, durability and recovery (Mohan et al., 1992), distributed execution (Van Steen and Tanenbaum, 2017), buffer management (Do et al., 2011), and high-concurrency updates (O’Neil et al., 1996; Xu et al., 2023). Vector similarity is also more useful when exposed as a composable operator (e.g., via DSL (Elastic, 2024)) to enable hybrid retrieval (text+vector), structured filtering, and reranking within a unified execution engine. To meet these system-level requirements, existing solutions can be broadly categorized into three architectural lines. Native vector databases, such as Milvus (Wang et al., 2021) and Pinecone (Pinecone, 2024), are designed for high-throughput, low-latency similarity search with elastic distributed scaling; their primary focus is vector-first index lifecycle management and distributed ANN execution, including segment organization, background compaction, and parallel search across shards. Relational databases extended with vector support, including pgvector (Yang et al., 2020), GaussDB-Vector (Sun et al., 2025), Blendhouse (Niu et al., 2025), Cosmos (Upreti et al., 2025), and MariaDB-Vector (Vector, 2023), embed vector data types and similarity operators into the relational stack; their central axis is tight integration with the storage manager, execution engine, and cost-based optimizer to enable composable plans with joins and predicates while controlling storage and computation overhead. Enterprise search engines such as OpenSearch (OpenSearch Project, 2024) and Elasticsearch (Elastic NV, 2024) incorporate vector retrieval into text-centric search pipelines; they emphasize the co-design of inverted and vector indexes to support hybrid ranking, filtering, and large-scale distributed search serving.

10. Conclusion

Modern AI applications have transformed search from a standalone nearest-neighbor operator into a production data-management problem: vector collections scale rapidly, queries mix vector similarity with diverse constraints, deployment modes shift between memory and disk as costs change, and operators still need mature search APIs and tooling. This paper presented UBASE, an OpenSearch-compatible AI search engine built from these observations. By combining a high-performance quantization-aware vector kernel, asynchronous SSD-resident graph traversal, and adaptive storage, UBASE supports both PB-scale ingestion-heavy deployments and latency-sensitive online serving. Our experience shows that modern AI search systems must treat vectors as first-class database primitives while preserving the operational ecosystem that production teams already depend on.

Appendix

Appendix A Ingestion side in UBASE

Write and indexing path.   The write path follows a staged lifecycle that makes fresh data searchable quickly while gradually turning it into serving-efficient indexes. \scriptsize1⃝ Data first enters through the standard OpenSearch ingestion interface; on refresh, new vectors are exposed as small fresh segments, avoiding heavyweight index construction on the critical ingestion path. \scriptsize2⃝ As ingestion continues, background merge compacts these segments to bound query fanout, which is essential for sustaining low latency under continuous writes. \scriptsize3⃝ During this process, UBASE upgrades the index representation with segment maturity: small segments are searched by direct scan, medium segments use IVF, and large stable segments are converted to graph indexes. \scriptsize4⃝ For graph-indexed segments, construction and merge are performed in the quantized space using SymRaBitQ, eliminating repeated full-precision vector materialization on the recurring merge path. \scriptsize5⃝ Once merged, the same segment can be placed in memory-resident, hybrid memory–SSD, or SSD-resident serving mode without reindexing or application migration.

Appendix B Serving side in UBASE

Read and serving path.   The read path preserves OpenSearch-style query semantics while hiding the heterogeneity of vector placement and execution. \scriptsize1⃝ A native DSL query is first parsed by the search coordinator and routed to the relevant shards. \scriptsize2⃝ Within each distributed query plan, UBASE jointly executes BM25 retrieval, vector similarity search, structured predicates, score fusion, and reranking, so applications do not need to issue separate requests or merge results across services. \scriptsize3⃝ Vector serving then adapts to placement: memory-resident segments use in-memory graph traversal, whereas SSD-resident graph records are accessed through a record-level buffer pool and coroutine-based asynchronous traversal that overlaps SSD reads with distance computation. \scriptsize4⃝ Output-heavy queries, including top-3 K and radial-style queries, are handled as increased serving pressure within the same execution framework rather than as a separate retrieval mode.

Appendix C OpenSearch-Compatible Hybrid Query

Listing 19 presents an example hybrid query in the native DSL. The query combines structured predicates, lexical matching, vector top-kk, score fusion, and a reranking pipeline without requiring applications to call separate retrieval services.

Appendix D RaBitQ, Graph, and IVF Background

This subsection gives the background that Sec. 4 intentionally keeps short. The main text focuses on SymRaBitQ and its integration into UBASE; here we spell out the baseline quantization and indexing mechanics.

D.1. RaBitQ and ExtRaBitQ

RaBitQ (Gao and Long, 2024) and ExtRaBitQ (Gao et al., 2025) estimate distances by reducing raw-vector scoring to inner-product estimation between normalized residual vectors. Given a centroid 𝒄\bm{c}, a raw data vector 𝒙r\bm{x}_{r}, and a raw query vector 𝒒r\bm{q}_{r}, define

(10) 𝒐=𝒙r−𝒄‖𝒙r−𝒄‖,𝒒=𝒒r−𝒄‖𝒒r−𝒄‖.\small\bm{o}=\frac{\bm{x}_{r}-\bm{c}}{\|\bm{x}_{r}-\bm{c}\|},\hskip 18.49988pt\bm{q}=\frac{\bm{q}_{r}-\bm{c}}{\|\bm{q}_{r}-\bm{c}\|}.

Then the squared Euclidean distance can be written as

(11) ‖𝒙r−𝒒r‖2=‖𝒙r−𝒄‖2+‖𝒒r−𝒄‖2−2​‖𝒙r−𝒄‖​‖𝒒r−𝒄‖​⟨𝒐,𝒒⟩,\small\|\bm{x}_{r}-\bm{q}_{r}\|^{2}=\|\bm{x}_{r}-\bm{c}\|^{2}+\|\bm{q}_{r}-\bm{c}\|^{2}-2\|\bm{x}_{r}-\bm{c}\|\|\bm{q}_{r}-\bm{c}\|\langle\bm{o},\bm{q}\rangle,

and inner-product scoring can be recovered by

(12) ⟨𝒙r,𝒒r⟩=⟨𝒙r,𝒄⟩−‖𝒄‖2+⟨𝒒r,𝒄⟩+‖𝒙r−𝒄‖​‖𝒒r−𝒄‖​⟨𝒐,𝒒⟩.\small\langle\bm{x}_{r},\bm{q}_{r}\rangle=\langle\bm{x}_{r},\bm{c}\rangle-\|\bm{c}\|^{2}+\langle\bm{q}_{r},\bm{c}\rangle+\|\bm{x}_{r}-\bm{c}\|\|\bm{q}_{r}-\bm{c}\|\langle\bm{o},\bm{q}\rangle.

Terms involving the stored data vector and centroid are precomputed, so the online problem is to estimate ⟨𝒐,𝒒⟩\langle\bm{o},\bm{q}\rangle.

RaBitQ builds a conceptual rotated codebook. Let

(13) 𝒢\displaystyle\mathcal{G} :={−2B−12+u|u=0,1,…,2B−1}D,\displaystyle:=\left\{-\frac{2^{B}-1}{2}+u~\middle|~u=0,1,\ldots,2^{B}-1\right\}^{D},
𝒢r\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{r} :={P​𝒚‖𝒚‖|𝒚∈𝒢},\displaystyle:=\left\{P\frac{\bm{y}}{\|\bm{y}\|}~\middle|~\bm{y}\in\mathcal{G}\right\},

where PP is a random orthogonal transformation matrix and BB is the number of bits per dimension. A vector is quantized by finding the nearest element of 𝒢r\mathcal{G}_{r}. Because explicitly materializing 𝒢r\mathcal{G}_{r} would require 2B​D2^{BD} candidates, RaBitQ applies the inverse rotation to the vector and searches in the unrotated integer lattice:

(14) arg​min𝐨¯∈𝒢r⁡‖𝐨¯−𝐨‖2=arg​max𝐲¯∈𝒢⁡⟨𝐲¯‖𝐲¯‖,P−1​𝐨⟩.\small\argmin_{\bar{\bm{o}}\in\mathcal{G}_{r}}\|\bar{\bm{o}}-\bm{o}\|^{2}=\argmax_{\bar{\bm{y}}\in\mathcal{G}}\left\langle\frac{\bar{\bm{y}}}{\|\bar{\bm{y}}\|},P^{-1}\bm{o}\right\rangle.

This yields a compact code 𝒖∈{0,…,2B−1}D\bm{u}\in\{0,\ldots,2^{B}-1\}^{D} and a quantized unit vector 𝒐¯\bar{\bm{o}}.

For two encoded vectors with integer codes 𝒖o\bm{u}_{o} and 𝒖q\bm{u}_{q}, define the centered code vectors 𝒖~o=𝒖o−(2B−1)​𝟏D/2\tilde{\bm{u}}_{o}=\bm{u}_{o}-(2^{B}-1)\bm{1}_{D}/2 and 𝒖~q=𝒖q−(2B−1)​𝟏D/2\tilde{\bm{u}}_{q}=\bm{u}_{q}-(2^{B}-1)\bm{1}_{D}/2. Since 𝒐¯=P​𝒖~o/‖𝒖~o‖\bar{\bm{o}}=P\tilde{\bm{u}}_{o}/\|\tilde{\bm{u}}_{o}\|, 𝒒¯=P​𝒖~q/‖𝒖~q‖\bar{\bm{q}}=P\tilde{\bm{u}}_{q}/\|\tilde{\bm{u}}_{q}\|, and PT​P=IP^{T}P=I, the code-only numerator in SymRaBitQ is

(15) ⟨𝒐¯,𝒒¯⟩=⟨𝒖~o,𝒖~q⟩‖𝒖~o‖​‖𝒖~q‖.\small\langle\bar{\bm{o}},\bar{\bm{q}}\rangle=\frac{\langle\tilde{\bm{u}}_{o},\tilde{\bm{u}}_{q}\rangle}{\|\tilde{\bm{u}}_{o}\|\,\|\tilde{\bm{u}}_{q}\|}.

For B=1B=1, the centered codes have only two signs, so Eq. (15) is equivalent to normalized sign agreement and can be computed from the Hamming distance between binary codes.

The original RaBitQ/ExtRaBitQ query estimator is asymmetric:

(16) ⟨𝒐,𝒒⟩^RaBitQ=⟨𝒐¯,𝒒⟩⟨𝒐¯,𝒐⟩.\small\widehat{\langle\bm{o},\bm{q}\rangle}_{\mathrm{RaBitQ}}=\frac{\langle\bar{\bm{o}},\bm{q}\rangle}{\langle\bar{\bm{o}},\bm{o}\rangle}.

The denominator is a per-vector constant, but the numerator still contains the raw query/residual vector. This is suitable for data-to-query scoring. It is not sufficient for graph construction and segment merge, where the hot loop compares one stored vector against other stored candidate vectors. SymRaBitQ keeps the same code construction but replaces Eq. (16) with the symmetric estimator in Eq. (2), so stored-vector comparisons use only codes and precomputed constants.

D.2. Graph Index Background

Graph-based ANN indexes represent each vector as a vertex and store a bounded set of outgoing neighbors. A query starts from one or more entry points and performs a greedy search: it keeps a candidate list, repeatedly expands the currently closest unvisited vertex, inserts its outgoing neighbors, and truncates the list to a configured search width. The quality of the graph determines whether this local greedy process quickly reaches the true nearest-neighbor region.

UBASE follows the DiskANN/Vamana-style construction process (Jayaram Subramanya et al., 2019). For an inserted vector, the builder first runs a greedy search on the current graph to collect a candidate set. It then applies RobustPrune, which keeps at most RR outgoing neighbors while removing candidates that are close to an already selected neighbor. In a typical pruning step, after selecting the current closest candidate 𝒑\bm{p} to the inserted vector 𝒐\bm{o}, another candidate 𝒗\bm{v} can be removed when α​d​(𝒑,𝒗)≤d⁡(𝒐,𝒗)\alpha\,d(\bm{p},\bm{v})\leq d(\bm{o},\bm{v}). This rule encourages sparse, diverse neighborhoods and approximates the sparse-neighborhood property used by proximity graphs. The builder also inserts backward edges; if a neighbor’s out-degree exceeds RR, it is pruned again. Recent theoretical analysis further shows why Vamana-style graphs are attractive among proximity graph families (Li et al., 2025).

In UBASE, graph building is additionally segment-aware. The system computes cluster centers on a sample, assigns each vector to its nearest centers, builds a subgraph inside each cluster, and merges the subgraphs by unioning edges. This keeps construction parallel and local while allowing large merged segments to obtain a high-quality graph. The main-text contribution is that every distance d⁡(⋅,⋅)d(\cdot,\cdot) in greedy search, pruning, and backward-edge repair is replaced by 𝖲𝗒𝗆𝖣𝗂𝗌𝗍B\mathsf{SymDist}_{B}.

D.3. IVF and FastScan Background

An inverted-file (IVF) index partitions vectors by KMeans centroids. Each centroid owns an inverted list containing the vectors assigned to it, usually represented as residuals relative to the centroid. At query time, the system first compares the query with all centroids, chooses the closest n𝑝𝑟𝑜𝑏𝑒n_{\mathit{probe}} lists, and scans only those lists. IVF is cheap to build and works well for medium-size segments because it reduces scan volume without paying the heavier graph-construction cost.

IVF is commonly paired with quantization. The query is encoded or transformed with respect to each probed centroid, and list entries are scored with compressed codes. FastScan-style methods (André et al., 2015; André et al., 2017; André et al., 2021) speed up this scan by preparing query-specific lookup tables and evaluating low-bit codes with SIMD-friendly operations. UBASE uses the same idea in a SymRaBitQ form: the first-bit code gives a very cheap coarse distance and bound, and the remaining bits are used only for candidates that survive coarse filtering.

Appendix E The Bounds of SymRaBitQ

We first show that SymRaBitQ admits a bounded error in the same spirit as RaBitQ (Gao and Long, 2024).

Let 𝒆1=𝒐−⟨𝒐,𝒒⟩​𝒒‖𝒐−⟨𝒐,𝒒⟩​𝒒‖\bm{e}_{1}=\dfrac{\bm{o}-\langle\bm{o},\bm{q}\rangle\bm{q}}{\|\bm{o}-\langle\bm{o},\bm{q}\rangle\bm{q}\|}, so that 𝒆1⟂𝒒\bm{e}_{1}\perp\bm{q}. Then we can decompose

(17) 𝒒¯\displaystyle\bar{\bm{q}} =(𝒒¯−⟨𝒒¯,𝒒⟩​𝒒−⟨𝒒¯,𝒆1⟩​𝒆1)+⟨𝒒¯,𝒒⟩​𝒒+⟨𝒒¯,𝒆1⟩​𝒆1,\displaystyle=\big(\bar{\bm{q}}-\langle\bar{\bm{q}},\bm{q}\rangle\bm{q}-\langle\bar{\bm{q}},\bm{e}_{1}\rangle\bm{e}_{1}\big)+\langle\bar{\bm{q}},\bm{q}\rangle\bm{q}+\langle\bar{\bm{q}},\bm{e}_{1}\rangle\bm{e}_{1},
𝒐\displaystyle\bm{o} =⟨𝒐,𝒒⟩​𝒒+⟨𝒐,𝒆1⟩​𝒆1.\displaystyle=\langle\bm{o},\bm{q}\rangle\bm{q}+\langle\bm{o},\bm{e}_{1}\rangle\bm{e}_{1}.

Consequently,

(18) ⟨𝒒¯,𝒐⟩\displaystyle\langle\bar{\bm{q}},\bm{o}\rangle =⟨𝒒¯,𝒒⟩​⟨𝒐,𝒒⟩+⟨𝒒¯,𝒆1⟩​⟨𝒐,𝒆1⟩\displaystyle=\langle\bar{\bm{q}},\bm{q}\rangle\langle\bm{o},\bm{q}\rangle+\langle\bar{\bm{q}},\bm{e}_{1}\rangle\langle\bm{o},\bm{e}_{1}\rangle
=⟨𝒒¯,𝒒⟩​⟨𝒐,𝒒⟩+⟨𝒒¯,𝒆1⟩​1−⟨𝒐,𝒒⟩2.\displaystyle=\langle\bar{\bm{q}},\bm{q}\rangle\langle\bm{o},\bm{q}\rangle+\langle\bar{\bm{q}},\bm{e}_{1}\rangle\sqrt{1-\langle\bm{o},\bm{q}\rangle^{2}}.

Thus,

(19) ⟨𝒒¯,𝒐⟩⟨𝒒¯,𝒒⟩=⟨𝒐,𝒒⟩+1−⟨𝒐,𝒒⟩2⋅⟨𝒒¯,𝒆1⟩⟨𝒒¯,𝒒⟩.\small\frac{\langle\bar{\bm{q}},\bm{o}\rangle}{\langle\bar{\bm{q}},\bm{q}\rangle}=\langle\bm{o},\bm{q}\rangle+\sqrt{1-\langle\bm{o},\bm{q}\rangle^{2}}\cdot\frac{\langle\bar{\bm{q}},\bm{e}_{1}\rangle}{\langle\bar{\bm{q}},\bm{q}\rangle}.

(20) ⟨𝒐¯,𝒒¯⟩⟨𝒐¯,𝒐⟩=⟨𝒐,𝒒¯⟩+1−⟨𝒐,𝒒¯⟩2⋅⟨𝒐¯,𝒆2⟩⟨𝒐¯,𝒐⟩.\small\frac{\langle\bar{\bm{o}},\bar{\bm{q}}\rangle}{\langle\bar{\bm{o}},\bm{o}\rangle}=\langle\bm{o},\bar{\bm{q}}\rangle+\sqrt{1-\langle\bm{o},\bar{\bm{q}}\rangle^{2}}\cdot\frac{\langle\bar{\bm{o}},\bm{e}_{2}\rangle}{\langle\bar{\bm{o}},\bm{o}\rangle}.

Combining the two identities, we obtain

−1−⟨𝒐,𝒒⟩2⋅⟨𝒒¯,𝒆1⟩⟨𝒒¯,𝒒⟩.\displaystyle-\sqrt{1-\langle\bm{o},\bm{q}\rangle^{2}}\cdot\frac{\langle\bar{\bm{q}},\bm{e}_{1}\rangle}{\langle\bar{\bm{q}},\bm{q}\rangle}.

Appendix F The Unbiasedness of SymRaBitQ

To prove the unbiasedness of SymRaBitQ, we first recall a standard concentration fact for Gaussian matrices.

Lemma 1.

For a d×dd\times d random matrix AA with i.i.d. entries from 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1), the normalized Gram matrix 1d​AT​A\frac{1}{d}A^{T}A concentrates around the identity; in particular,

(23) {1d​AT​A−Id}i​j=O⁡(1d).\small\left\{\frac{1}{d}A^{T}A-I_{d}\right\}_{ij}=O\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\right).

Equivalently, 1d​A\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}A is nearly orthogonal when dd is large.

Proof.

The entries of AT​AA^{T}A are

(24) (AT​A)i​j=∑k=1dak​i​ak​j.\small(A^{T}A)_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^{d}a_{ki}a_{kj}.

For i=ji=j, 𝔼⁡[(AT​A)i​i]=d\mathbb{E}[(A^{T}A)_{ii}]=d and Var⁡((AT​A)i​i)=2​d\mathrm{Var}((A^{T}A)_{ii})=2d; for i≠ji\neq j, 𝔼⁡[(AT​A)i​j]=0\mathbb{E}[(A^{T}A)_{ij}]=0 and Var⁡((AT​A)i​j)=d\mathrm{Var}((A^{T}A)_{ij})=d. Therefore, after normalization by dd, both diagonal and off-diagonal entries have fluctuations on the order of 1/d1/\sqrt{d}, i.e.,

(25) {1d​AT​A−Id}i​j=O⁡(1d),\small\left\{\frac{1}{d}A^{T}A-I_{d}\right\}_{ij}=O\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\right),

which implies that 1d​A\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}A is close to an orthogonal matrix for large dd. ∎

With Lemma 1, we can treat the orthogonal matrix PP in RaBitQ as a properly normalized Gaussian random matrix. Then

(26) ⟨𝒐¯,𝒒¯⟩\displaystyle\langle\bar{\bm{o}},\bar{\bm{q}}\rangle =∑i=1dξ⁡(𝒒¯​[i],𝒐¯​[i])\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\xi(\bar{\bm{q}}[i],\bar{\bm{o}}[i])
=1d​∑i=1dξ⁡(hi∗​(𝒒′),hi∗​(𝒙)),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\xi\big(h_{i}^{*}(\bm{q}^{\prime}),h_{i}^{*}(\bm{x})\big),

where hi∗​(𝒙)h_{i}^{*}(\bm{x}) is the inner product with a standard Gaussian random vector 𝒂\bm{a} whose entries satisfy ai∼i.i.d.𝒩⁡(0,1)a_{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i.i.d.}}{{\sim}}\mathcal{N}(0,1). The function ξ⁡(X1,X2)\xi(X_{1},X_{2}) is defined as

(27) ξ⁡(X1,X2)={1,sign⁡(X1)=sign⁡(X2),−1,sign⁡(X1)≠sign⁡(X2).\small\xi(X_{1},X_{2})=\begin{cases}1,&\mathrm{sign}(X_{1})=\mathrm{sign}(X_{2}),\\ -1,&\mathrm{sign}(X_{1})\neq\mathrm{sign}(X_{2}).\end{cases}

By Lemma 1 in (Zhao et al., 2023b), 𝔼⁡[ξ⁡(X1,X2)]=1−2​θπ\mathbb{E}[\xi(X_{1},X_{2})]=1-\frac{2\theta}{\pi}, where θ\theta is the angle between 𝒒\bm{q} and 𝒙\bm{x}. Hence 𝔼⁡[⟨𝒐¯,𝒒¯⟩]=1−2​θπ\mathbb{E}[\langle\bar{\bm{o}},\bar{\bm{q}}\rangle]=1-\frac{2\theta}{\pi}. Moreover, ⟨𝒐¯,𝒐⟩\langle\bar{\bm{o}},\bm{o}\rangle and ⟨𝒒¯,𝒒⟩\langle\bar{\bm{q}},\bm{q}\rangle are both close to 2π\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}, so

(28) 𝔼⁡[⟨𝒐¯,𝒒¯⟩⟨𝒐¯,𝒐⟩​⟨𝒒¯,𝒒⟩]≈π2−θ.\small\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\langle\bar{\bm{o}},\bar{\bm{q}}\rangle}{\langle\bar{\bm{o}},\bm{o}\rangle\langle\bar{\bm{q}},\bm{q}\rangle}\right]\approx\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta.

Let t=π2−θt=\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta. In high dimensions, two unrelated vectors tend to be nearly orthogonal, so tt is typically close to 00. When t=0t=0, we have ⟨𝒐,𝒒⟩=0\langle\bm{o},\bm{q}\rangle=0 and SymRaBitQ is unbiased. When t≠0t\neq 0 but small,

(29) 𝔼⁡[⟨𝒐¯,𝒒¯⟩⟨𝒐¯,𝒐⟩​⟨𝒒¯,𝒒⟩]−⟨𝒐,𝒒⟩=t−sin⁡(t)=O⁡(t3),\small\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\langle\bar{\bm{o}},\bar{\bm{q}}\rangle}{\langle\bar{\bm{o}},\bm{o}\rangle\langle\bar{\bm{q}},\bm{q}\rangle}\right]-\langle\bm{o},\bm{q}\rangle=t-\sin(t)=O(t^{3}),

which is negligible as t→0t\to 0. Therefore, SymRaBitQ is approximately unbiased in typical high-dimensional settings.

Fig. 20 further validates the unbiasedness analysis in practice. Across both settings, most samples concentrate around the y=xy=x line, and the fitted slope/intercept are close to the ideal values (slope 11, intercept 00). This shows that the estimated distance tracks the real distance well, with only limited deviation in the low-distance region.

Appendix G Controlled Benchmark Configuration

Table 5 summarizes the resource provisioning and index/tuning configurations used in the controlled benchmark deployments. For Elasticsearch and UBASE, the coordinator nodes run query coordination only; the data nodes store and serve the vector index. PostgreSQL runs on a large host with cgroup limits to match the aggregate compute and memory budget of the corresponding data tier. Milvus uses its standard role-separated deployment. Across distributed systems, Wiki and GIST use one shard with three total copies, while Cohere and the in-house dataset use three shards without replicas. PostgreSQL/VectorChord runs as a single-node system. To put each distributed system in its optimized query-serving state, we consolidate each shard into a single segment before evaluation for Elasticsearch, Milvus, and UBASE. For PostgreSQL, we follow VectorChord’s official performance-tuning guidance99 9 https://docs.vectorchord.ai/vectorchord/usage/performance-tuning.html and apply the parameters listed below: max_worker_processes = 80, max_parallel_workers = 71, max_parallel_maintenance_workers = 71, effective_io _concurrency = 20, maintenance_io_concurrency = 20, jit= off, and shared_buffers = 460GB

Appendix H Operating-Cost Configuration

The operating-cost comparison in Table 4 charges only the serving tier that physically stores or serves the in-house dataset. Auxiliary components, such as coordinators, proxies, index nodes, and mixcoord nodes, are excluded because their overhead is shared or amortized and does not scale directly with dataset size. Milvus, Elasticsearch, UBASE (Memory-only), and PostgreSQL use the in-house serving footprint shown in Table 5; PostgreSQL is charged by its cgroup-limited serving footprint.1010 10 A larger host may be used for deployment, but the resource and cost model charges only the cgroup-limited serving footprint. All charged nodes use the same commercial cloud instance family unless otherwise stated. UBASE (Disk-only) uses 3 ×\times 2C16GiB data nodes because only the minimal index structures are memory-resident, while the remaining data are stored on disk.
